Q1.answer: Ten presidential documents in the section 338 series are published through today (Nov 14, 2026). Each date is signed / published (91 FR first page), then what it does, then the operative date and what that date is measured against. (1) Proc. 11046 (alcoholic beverages), FR Doc 2026-14991, 91 FR 46639; signed July 20; published July 23; imposes 50% on Canadian products in Annex II; effective 12:01 a.m. ET Aug 19, 2026 (clauses (1),(3); 46641), measured against goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption. (2) Proc. 11047 (dairy), 2026-14992, 91 FR 46653; signed July 20; published July 23; 50% on Annex II products; effective 12:01 a.m. Aug 19 (entry/withdrawal event). (3) Proc. 11048 (motor vehicles), 2026-14997, 91 FR 46663; signed July 20; published July 23; 50% on Annex II products; effective 12:01 a.m. Aug 19 (entry/withdrawal event). (4) Proc. 11056 (temporary suspension), 2026-17294, 91 FR 54789; signed Aug 18; published Aug 24; suspends for 3 days; clause (1) sets the effective date of 11046-11048 at 12:01 a.m. Aug 22, 2026 and amends the Annex II chapeau of each (54790); the date is measured against entry/withdrawal. (5) Proc. 11061 (alcoholic beverages import exclusion), 2026-18835, 91 FR 58311; signed Sept 8; published Sept 14; excludes the Annex products; effective for goods imported on or after 12:01 a.m. Sept 29 (clause (1), 58312), so the event is importation (arrival), not entry. (6) Proc. 11062 (dairy exclusion), 2026-18836, 91 FR 58319; signed Sept 8; published Sept 14; same structure; effective goods imported on/after 12:01 a.m. Sept 29 (import event). (7) Proc. 11063 (motor vehicles exclusion), 2026-18837, 91 FR 58325; signed Sept 8; published Sept 14; same structure; import event 12:01 a.m. Sept 29. (8) Proc. 11064 (alcoholic beverages scope), 2026-18838, 91 FR 58331; signed Sept 8; published Sept 14; Part A products made subject to the 50% duty, Part B products no longer subject (clause (1), 58332); effective 12:01 a.m. Sept 15 (entry/withdrawal). (9) Proc. 11065 (motor vehicles scope), 2026-18839, 91 FR 58339; signed Sept 8; filed Sept 11 11:15 a.m.; published Sept 14; Part A made subject to 50%, Part B no longer subject (clause (1), 58340); effective 12:01 a.m. Sept 15 (entry/withdrawal). (10) Proc. 11076 (further motor vehicles scope), 2026-22292, 91 FR 68861; signed Oct 23; filed Oct 29 11:15 a.m.; published Oct 30; Part A products no longer subject, Part B products made subject (clause (1), 68862); effective 12:01 a.m. Oct 30 (entry/withdrawal). Product-group changes: Alcoholic beverages: 11046 created the Annex II list; 11064 changed Parts A and B (Sept 15); 11061 moved Annex products from the 50% duty to an import ban (Sept 29); 11056 changed only the start date. Dairy: 11047 created the list; 11062 moved its Annex products to the import ban (Sept 29); 11056 changed only the start date; no dairy scope proclamation exists. Motor vehicles: 11048 created the list; 11065 added Part A and removed Part B (Sept 15); 11076 removed Part A and added Part B (Oct 30); 11063 moved its Annex products to the import ban (Sept 29); 11056 changed only the start date. I read the full operative text of 11046, 11056, 11061, 11064, 11065 and 11076; for 11047, 11048, 11062 and 11063 I checked the operative date and transition clauses only.
Q1.uncertainty: Annex II and Parts A and B are images and cannot be read, so which products are on each list comes from the scenario statements. Recitals in 11064, 11065 and 11076 still say the duties were effective Aug 19 (see Q11). The date of 11056 publication (Aug 24) is after its signing; its own suspension start is not stated separately.

Q2.answer: (a) Entry 1 (2:00 p.m. Aug 20): $0. Entry 2 (11:59 p.m. Aug 21): $0. Entry 3 (12:01 a.m. Aug 22): 50% x $40,000 = $20,000. Controlling text: 11056 clause (1) (the effective date of the duties under 11046 is 12:01 a.m. Aug 22), with clause (2) directing that collection be suspended; 11064 recital 4 says the 3-day suspension lapsed at 12:01 a.m. Aug 22. (b) 11046 printed Aug 19 in the 50% clause (1), the HTSUS clause (3) and the recital in clause (9). 11056 clause (1) amended only the Annex II chapeau of 11046, 11047 and 11048 by replacing August 19, 2026 with August 22, 2026. The body clauses (1), (3) and (9) of 11046 were not amended and still say Aug 19. What resolves the difference: 11056 is the later instrument, states the Aug 22 date expressly, and clause (5) of 11056 supersedes inconsistent earlier provisions. Later proclamations confirm Aug 22 (11064 recital 4; 11065 recital 4; 11076 recital 4). (c) The broker's deposit on entry 1 was not owed under the Aug 22 date. Clause (4) of 11056 says that to the extent implementation requires a refund of duties collected, refunds shall be processed under applicable law and CBP's standard procedures. The documents give no other refund mechanics. (d) No further presidential action was needed to start the duties. The Aug 18 proclamation itself set the Aug 22 start. Later documents say that Canada on Aug 21 reneged on its commitment and did not remove the discrimination, so at 12:01 a.m. Aug 22 the 3-day suspension lapsed and the duties became effective (11064 recitals 3-4; 11065 recitals 3-4). They say nothing further about the days before Aug 22 beyond that. (e) Section 9 of 11046 and clause (10) say the duties may not take effect earlier than 30 days after the finding. The finding is dated July 20 (signing). July 20 plus 30 days is Aug 19 (July 21-31 is 11 days; Aug 1-19 is 19 days; total 30). Aug 19 was therefore the earliest permitted date, and the proclamation printed it.
Q2.basis: FR Doc 2026-14991 (91 FR 46639): recital 9 (46640), clause (10) (46640) on the 30-day rule, clause (1) (46641), clause (3) (46641), clause (9) (46642), signed July 20 (46642); FR Doc 2026-17294 (91 FR 54789): recital 4 and clause (1) (54790), clause (2) suspension of collection (54790), clause (4) refunds (54791), clause (5) supersession (54791); FR Doc 2026-18838 (91 FR 58331), recitals 2-4 (58331); FR Doc 2026-18835 (91 FR 58311), recitals 3-4 (58311).
Q2.uncertainty: The text does not say how the broker's deposit on entry 1 was handled or what CBP's standard refund procedure is; it says only that refunds shall be processed under applicable law. The documents do not expressly address whether entry 1 was ever liquidated or whether any duty was collected on Aug 19-21. The exact Annex II list (wine in Annex II) is an image; I accepted the scenario's statement that wine is listed.

Q3.answer: (a) A. Admitted: yes, it was imported Sept 10, before the Sept 29 ban (11061 clause (1), import-based). Section 338 duty: 50% x $30,000 = $15,000. The 50% rate is 11046 clause (1) (entry Sept 14, after Aug 22). B. Admitted: yes; imported Sept 27 (before Sept 29) and not withdrawn for consumption before Sept 29, so 11061 clause (2) keeps the 50% rate. Section 338 duty: 50% x $30,000 = $15,000. C. Admitted: yes; it arrived at 11:30 p.m. Sept 28, before the 12:01 a.m. Sept 29 cut-off, so clause (2) applies and the 50% rate continues; the 9:00 a.m. Sept 29 entry does not change this. Section 338 duty: $15,000. D. Not admissible: it arrived at 12:30 a.m. Sept 29, after the cut-off, and is subject to the import ban in clause (1) of 11061. No section 338 duty is owed because no entry for consumption can be made. (b) Shipment E arrived Sept 25 and was admitted to the FTZ. Clause (4) of 11046 requires privileged foreign status for goods admitted after the effective date, and says the goods are subject upon entry for consumption to the ad valorem rate for their classification. Because E was imported before Sept 29, it is not subject to the import ban. The Oct 6 entry therefore bears the 50% duty: $15,000. (c) Under clause (9)(b) of 11061, if the ban is invalidated as to any import, the 50% duty under 11046 applies to that import, and the duty is collected prospectively from the date of invalidation. Imports after the ruling therefore bear the 50% section 338 duty and are not banned. (d) No. Clause (3) of 11061 says the proclamation does not otherwise affect the products that are subject to 11046, other than moving the Annex products to the ban. Listed Canadian alcoholic products not in the Annex remain subject to the 50% duty, as modified by 11064.
Q3.basis: FR Doc 2026-14991 clauses (1), (4) (91 FR 46641), 2026-18835 (91 FR 58312-58313): clause (1) (import-based ban from 12:01 a.m. Sept 29), clause (2) (products imported before Sept 29 remain at 50%), clause (3) (no other effect), clause (9)(a)-(b) (severability, 58313-58314); FR Doc 2026-18838 (91 FR 58331) for Parts A and B; FR Doc 2026-22292 not relevant to beer.
Q3.uncertainty: Clause (2) of 11061 refers to goods imported but not yet entered or withdrawn from warehouse. It does not mention FTZ admission, so shipment E's position depends on reading clause (2) with the FTZ rule in 11046 clause (4). The beer's own 301 duty is outside this question but is a separate additional duty (10% for Canada, see Q6). The Annex lists are images.

Q4.answer: (a) Sept 10, 2026: X: section 232 25% x $100,000 = $25,000; section 338 $0; total additional $25,000. Y: section 232 $25,000; section 338 $0; total $25,000. Z: section 232 $25,000; section 338 $0; total $25,000. (b) Oct 1, 2026: X: section 232 $25,000 plus section 338 50% x $100,000 = $50,000; total $75,000. Y: section 232 $25,000; section 338 $0 (the dairy proclamation was never amended by a scope proclamation); total $25,000. Z: section 232 $25,000 plus section 338 50% x $100,000 = $50,000; total $75,000. (c) Sept 10: clause (2) of 11046 (91 FR 46641) says the duties 'shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232'; clause (2) of 11047 (46655) and clause (2) of 11048 say the same. Oct 1: clause (1) of 11064 (91 FR 58332) and of 11065 (58340) say the duties under 11046/11048, as modified, 'shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232', effective 12:01 a.m. Sept 15, and clause (7) of 11064 (58333) supersedes inconsistent provisions of previous proclamations. X is not on any Part A or B list, so it remains subject to 50%. Y is in no scope proclamation, so clause (2) of 11047 still applies. Z is not in Part A or B of 11065, so it remains subject to 50%.
Q4.basis: FR Doc 2026-14991 clause (2) (91 FR 46641); FR Doc 2026-14992 clause (2) (91 FR 46655); FR Doc 2026-14997 clause (2) (91 FR 46665); FR Doc 2026-18838 clause (1) (91 FR 58332) and clause (7) (58333); FR Doc 2026-18839 clause (1) (91 FR 58340); FR Doc 2026-22292 for the Oct 30 change, which does not affect these products. The 232 rate of 25% is the scenario's assumption, not verified against a 232 document for these products. Section 301 is not computed here.
Q4.uncertainty: The statement in 11064 and 11065 that the 338 duty applies in addition to 232 conflicts with clause (2) of the original proclamations. I resolved it by treating the later clauses as superseding (clause (7) of 11064; clause (9) of 11048 which is parallel). The documents do not expressly say that this was meant to apply to products already subject to 232 duties. Which Annex II products also have Part A or B status is an image, so the answer assumes none for X, Y or Z.

Q5.answer: (a) P: 3:00 p.m. Sept 14: no (not subject; P is first listed in Part A effective 12:01 a.m. Sept 15). 12:01 a.m. Sept 15: yes (Part A of 11065). Oct 29 4:00 p.m.: yes (still in Part A; 11076 does not list P). Oct 30 12:01 a.m.: yes. Nov 3: yes. Q: Sept 14 3:00 p.m.: yes (Annex II of 11048 and not yet removed). Sept 15 12:01 a.m.: no (Part B of 11065 removed it). Oct 29: no. Oct 30: no. Nov 3: no. R: Sept 14: yes. Sept 15: yes. Oct 29: yes. Oct 30 12:01 a.m.: no (Part A of 11076 removed it). Nov 3: no. S: Sept 14: no. Sept 15: no. Oct 29 4:00 p.m.: no. Oct 30 12:01 a.m.: yes (Part B of 11076). Nov 3: yes. The 50% duty in every case is the section 338 duty under 11048 as modified; no section 232 duty is involved. (b) 11076 (October) was signed Oct 23, filed for public inspection Oct 29 at 11:15 a.m., and published in the Federal Register Oct 30 (91 FR 68861). It applies from 12:01 a.m. Oct 30, for goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse on or after that time. The scope proclamations apply prospectively. They do not reach entries made before their effective times, and neither 11065 nor 11076 contains a refund provision (no refund text in either). (c) P became dutiable 7 days after signing (signed Sept 8, effective Sept 15 12:01 a.m.). S also became dutiable 7 days after signing (signed Oct 23, effective Oct 30 12:01 a.m.). The scope proclamations quote the statutory rule that additional duties may not take effect earlier than 30 days after the finding (11065 recital at 58340; 11076 recital at 68862), but neither explains how a 7-day effective date fits that rule. Neither says the 30-day limit is measured from the July 20 finding or treated as already satisfied. The documents are silent on the reconciliation.
Q5.basis: FR Doc 2026-18839 (91 FR 58339): signing Sept 8 (58341), clause (1) (58340), clause (2) (58340), filing 9-11-26 (58346); FR Doc 2026-22292 (91 FR 68861): signing Oct 23 (68863), clause (1) (68862), filing 10-29-26 11:15 a.m. (68871), recital on the 30-day limit (68862); FR Doc 2026-14991 clause (10) (91 FR 46640) for the statutory rule as applied to the July 20 finding.
Q5.uncertainty: The Annex I parts are images, so the list memberships in the scenario are taken as given. The reconciliation with the 30-day rule is not explained in the text. I could not find any statement on refunds in the scope proclamations, so the answer is that none is stated.

Q6.answer: Section 301 duty on $100,000 at MFN 4%, and total MFN plus 301. (1) Switzerland: 12.5% net of MFN, so 301 = 12.5% - 4% = 8.5% x $100,000 = $8,500; total = $4,000 MFN + $8,500 = $12,500. (2) Norway: 12.5% flat; 301 = $12,500; total $4,000 + $12,500 = $16,500. (3) UK: 10% flat; 301 = $10,000; total $14,000. (4) Germany (a member state of the EU): 10% net of MFN; 301 = 10% - 4% = 6% = $6,000; total $10,000. (5) Taiwan: 10% net of MFN; 301 = $6,000; total $10,000. (6) Turkiye: 12.5% flat; 301 = $12,500; total $16,500. (7) Japan: 12.5% net of MFN; 301 = $8,500; total $12,500. (8) Liechtenstein: not one of the 60 investigated economies (not named in the notice); no 301 duty; total $4,000 MFN only. (9) Hong Kong: 12.5% flat; 301 = $12,500; total $16,500. (10) India: 10% flat; 301 = $10,000; total $14,000. (b) Germany, MFN 12%: 10% net; MFN is at or above 10%, so 301 = $0. Japan, MFN 12%: 12.5% net; 301 = 0.5% x $100,000 = $500. Taiwan, MFN exactly 10%: 0. South Korea, MFN 10%: 12.5% net; 301 = 2.5% x $100,000 = $2,500. Switzerland, MFN 0: 12.5% net; 301 = $12,500. (c) Differences from the June 5 proposal (which proposed 10% for listed economies and 12.5% for all others, all as flat rates, with no net-of-MFN structure): Germany (EU) and Taiwan: the rate stayed 10% but became net of MFN. Japan and Switzerland: the rate stayed 12.5% but became net of MFN. India: changed from 12.5% to 10% (flat); the reason stated is India's adoption of a forced labor import prohibition after the June 5 publication (notice, India determination). UK: 10% in both. Norway, Hong Kong and Turkiye: 12.5% in both. Liechtenstein was not in the proposal.
Q6.basis: FR Doc 2026-15274 (memorandum, 91 FR 47717) and FR Doc 2026-15181 section 1(a)(i)-(iii) as quoted at 91 FR 47319-47320; per-economy determinations at 91 FR 47323 (EU, line 747), 47324 (Hong Kong, line 811; India, line 823; Japan, line 875), 47326 (Norway, line 1023), 47327 (Switzerland, line 1180; Taiwan, line 1197; Turkiye, line 1242 (47327-28)), 47328 (UK, line 1271); the net-of-MFN rule in note (k) (91 FR 47394); the June proposal at 91 FR 34274 (rates) (FR Doc 2026-11296). Liechtenstein does not appear in either notice.
Q6.uncertainty: The annex exemptions for each economy are images and could reduce the duty on particular products; I assume none applies. The rate for the EU applies to products of member states; I treated Germany as an EU member state.

Q7.answer: (a) France (EU, 10% net of MFN): column 1 = 3 cents/kg x 2,000 kg = $60; AVE = $60 / $12,000 = 0.5%; 301 = 10% - 0.5% = 9.5% x $12,000 = $1,140. (b) Column 1 = 4% x $20,000 ($800) plus 25 cents x 4,000 kg ($1,000) = $1,800 = 9% AVE. Italy (EU, net 10%): 301 = 1% x $20,000 = $200. Japan (net 12.5%): 301 = 3.5% x $20,000 = $700. Brazil (12.5% flat, not net): 301 = 12.5% x $20,000 = $2,500. (c) AVE = $2,200 / $20,000 = 11%. Taiwan (net 10%): 11% is at or above 10%, so 301 = $0. Switzerland (net 12.5%): 301 = 1.5% x $20,000 = $300. (d) The rule for non-ad valorem (specific or compound) column 1 rates is in the HTS note at 91 FR 47394 (note (k), for EU, Japan, Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan): AVE = column 1 duty / customs value, with the example at the end of the note. The result for a net-of-MFN product at or above the cap is in the same note (headings 9903.05.39 and 9903.05.76 for the 10% cap, and 9903.05.49, 9903.05.71 and 9903.05.74 for the 12.5% cap: where column 1 is at or above the cap, the additional rate is zero) and in section 1(a)(ii) of the memorandum at 91 FR 47320 (where MFN is at or above 10%, the 301 tariff is zero).
Q7.basis: FR Doc 2026-15181 note (k) (91 FR 47394, lines 2824-2837) and the cap sentences at lines 2838-2845; memorandum section 1(a)(ii) at 91 FR 47320 (FR Doc 2026-15274 quoted in the notice); FR Doc 2026-15181 per-economy determinations (France and Italy are EU; Brazil at 91 FR 47322, line 605).
Q7.uncertainty: The note states the cap sentences for particular heading numbers; I inferred the zero result at or above the cap from the 'sum equals X' wording, which is not stated as a separate rule for the at-or-above case in note (k) itself. Annex exemptions (image) not checked for these products.

Q8.answer: Each shipment: product of the Dominican Republic, 12.5% flat, $80,000: duty = $10,000 unless exempt. (1) Loaded July 22 on a vessel at Caucedo, direct to Miami, entered July 29: not exempt, because the in-transit exemption needs entry before 12:01 a.m. July 28. Duty $10,000. (2) Same vessel, entered 3:00 p.m. July 27: exempt, because it was loaded before 12:01 a.m. July 24, was in transit, and was entered before 12:01 a.m. July 28. Duty $0. (3) Entered 12:01 a.m. July 28: not before 12:01 a.m. July 28; duty $10,000. (4) Loaded 6:00 a.m. July 24 (after the 12:01 a.m. July 24 start): no transit exemption; entered July 27; duty $10,000. (5) Entered July 23: before the effective date; duty $0. (6) Arrived in June, in bond, withdrawn July 26: the duty applies to withdrawals on or after 12:01 a.m. July 24 and the transit exemption does not cover warehoused goods; duty $10,000. (7) Air freight loaded on an aircraft at 9:00 p.m. July 23, entered July 25: the transit exemption refers only to loading onto a vessel, so the text does not reach air freight; on the text as written the duty is $10,000 (flagged as a gap). (b) The rule for goods in transit is in the DATES paragraph of the notice (91 FR 47318): goods loaded onto a vessel at the port of loading and in transit on the final mode of transit before 12:01 a.m. July 24, and entered or withdrawn before 12:01 a.m. July 28, are not subject. (c) The memorandum was signed July 23, 2026 (91 FR 47717; published July 28). The USTR notice is 91 FR 47318, published July 28; duties apply to goods entered or withdrawn on or after 12:01 a.m. July 24, 2026. (d) Patented pharmaceutical under 9903.04.62: the notice does not mention heading 9903.04.62. It lists pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical ingredients among the additional products exempted (91 FR 47331, lines 1673-1674), but the exemption list is an image. If the article is within that exemption, the 301 duty is $0 on both July 30 and Aug 3. If not, it is $10,000 on both dates. The text does not decide which.
Q8.basis: FR Doc 2026-15181 (91 FR 47318): DATES (July 24 start and transit exemption), Dominican Republic determination at 91 FR 47323 (line 694, 12.5% flat), note 52 (91 FR 47352) and note 52(f) (91 FR 47362-63), pharmaceutical exemption discussion at 91 FR 47331 and 47332; FR Doc 2026-15274 (91 FR 47717) signed July 23 (47717 metadata).
Q8.uncertainty: The aircraft case is a gap: the transit rule says vessel only. The pharmaceutical heading 9903.04.62 does not appear in the text I could read; the 232 pharmaceutical proclamation (11020, see FR Doc 2026-19498) was not reviewed. The Annex exemption list is an image.

Q9.answer: (a) Assembled in Thailand under 9802.00.80: the duty applies to the value of the article assembled abroad less the U.S. content: $100,000 - $35,000 = $65,000. Thailand is 12.5% flat. 301 = 12.5% x $65,000 = $8,125. (b) Repairs in Israel under 9802.00.50: the duty applies to the value of repairs only ($6,000). Israel is 12.5% flat. 301 = 12.5% x $6,000 = $750. The $150,000 U.S. machine is not dutiable. (c) Mexico is 10% flat. (i) Entered free under USMCA: MFN $0; 301 = 10% x $50,000 = $5,000; total $5,000. (ii) No USMCA claim: MFN 5% x $50,000 = $2,500; 301 = $5,000; total $7,500. (d) A Japanese passenger car under 9903.94.01: 301 = $0, because note 52(f)(2) excludes headings 9903.94.01 and related headings from the 301 duty. (e) Brazil, 12.5% flat, $100,000: the note (f) exclusion list names specific 232 headings. A heading not named in note (f) is not excluded by the text read, so 301 = 12.5% x $100,000 = $12,500 (subject to the uncertainty below). (f) June 5 proposal: it excluded all articles and parts of articles subject to section 232 tariffs, informational materials, donations, accompanied baggage and USMCA-compliant goods of Canada or Mexico (91 FR 34274 and 34276). Adopted text: note 52(f) excludes only listed 232 headings (aluminum, steel and copper 9903.82 headings, passenger vehicles, parts, wood, trucks and so on) (47362-63); note 52(a) excludes personal-use accompanied baggage (47352). The operative text read does not contain an informational-materials or donations exemption, nor a general 232 exclusion, nor a USMCA exemption. The notice's summary says the proposal's exemptions 'included' 232 articles and informational materials and donations (47318).
Q9.basis: FR Doc 2026-15181 note 52(a) (91 FR 47352) and the 9802 rule at lines 2329-2334 (47352); note 52(f) (47362-63) and 52(f)(2) for 9903.94.01; Thailand determination (47327, line 1221); Israel (47324, line 868); Brazil (47322, line 605); Mexico (47325, line 965; 10% list in the memorandum at 47320); FR Doc 2026-11296 (91 FR 34274-34276).
Q9.uncertainty: Part (e) depends on whether a 232 heading not named in note (f) is nevertheless excluded by the summary sentence at 91 FR 47318 and the statement at 47330 about 232 products; the operative text does not say so. Part (c) assumes no USMCA carve-out; the June proposal had one, and the adopted operative text does not, but Annex I/II images could contain one. Informational materials and donations may be in Annex images.

Q10.answer: Scenario 1 (aluminum extrusions, 232 50% on $200,000; MFN 3% = $6,000; section 301 = $0 because note (f)(1) excludes 9903.82.02 articles). (a) Sept 10, 2026: MFN $6,000; section 232 $100,000; section 338 $0 (11048 clause (2) excludes 232 articles until 11065 takes effect); section 301 $0; total $106,000. (b) Sept 16, 2026: MFN $6,000; section 232 $100,000; section 338 50% x $200,000 = $100,000 (11065 clause (1), effective Sept 15); section 301 $0; total $206,000. Scenario 2 (rye whisky, $60,000, MFN free, section 301 at Canada's 10%, no USMCA carve-out in the text read). (c) USMCA-free entry on Sept 1: section 338 50% x $60,000 = $30,000; section 301 10% x $60,000 = $6,000; total $36,000. (d) No USMCA claim, Sept 1: section 338 $30,000; section 301 $6,000; total $36,000. (e) Arrival Oct 2: after the 12:01 a.m. Sept 29 cut-off the goods are excluded from importation (11061 clause (1)); no duty is assessed because they cannot be entered; section 338 $0; section 301 $0; total $0. (f) Under EO 14389 (signed Feb 20, 2026), the IEEPA duties under EO 14193 (northern border), as amended by 14231, 14325 and 14329, are no longer in effect and are no longer collected. The temporary import surcharge (proclamation 11012) ran from Feb 24 to 12:01 a.m. July 24, 2026 (clause (7)), and had expired. Neither applies to Canadian goods entered in September 2026, on the FR record.
Q10.basis: FR Doc 2026-14991 clause (2) (91 FR 46641); FR Doc 2026-18839 clause (1) (91 FR 58340); FR Doc 2026-18835 clause (1) (91 FR 58312); FR Doc 2026-15181 note (f)(1) (91 FR 47362) and note 52(a); FR Doc 2026-03832 (EO 14389, 91 FR 9437) Sec. 1 and 2(a) at 9437-9438; FR Doc 2026-03824 (proclamation 11012, 91 FR 9339) clause (7) at 9343 and exception (k)/(l) at 9341.
Q10.uncertainty: The USMCA point under 301 (scenario 2 (c) and (d)) is open: the adopted notice has no USMCA exemption in the text I read, while the June proposal did. Annex lists are images. EO 14389 does not say the exact collection-stop date; 'as soon as practicable' is used. The IEEPA termination is an FR fact; I did not verify court rulings, which are outside the FR.

Q11.answer: Discrepancies found, each listed once. (1) 11064 and 11065 recital 1 say the section 338 duties were 'effective August 19, 2026', but the same proclamations' recital 4 says the 3-day suspension lapsed and the duties became effective at 12:01 a.m. Aug 22 (11064: 91 FR 58331; 11065: 91 FR 58339 recital 1 and recital 4). Also 11076 recital 1 (91 FR 68861) says Aug 19. (2) 11056 clause (1) says the effective date of 11046-11048 'shall be' Aug 22 and says the Annex II chapeau is amended. But the operative body clauses of 11046, 11047 and 11048 (clause (1), clause (3) and the clause (9) recital) still say Aug 19 and were not amended (11046 at 91 FR 46641). (3) 11064 and 11065 clause (1) says the section 338 duties 'shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232'. Clause (2) of 11046-11048 says the duties 'shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232' (91 FR 46641, 46655, 46665). The later proclamations do not say they change clause (2), though clause (7) of 11064 supersedes inconsistent provisions. (4) The USTR notice's summary (91 FR 47318, lines 171-173) says the June proposal's exemptions 'included' all articles and parts subject to section 232 tariffs. The adopted operative note 52(f) (91 FR 47362-63) lists only specific 232 headings. The notice's own text at 47335 (line 2031) refers only to auto parts already subject to 232 being exempt. (5) The notice's summary of the June proposal's exemptions (91 FR 47318) omits the proposal's exemption for USMCA-compliant goods of Canada and Mexico (91 FR 34276, lines 567-571), and the adopted operative text contains no such exemption. (6) The notice's summary (91 FR 47318, lines 171-173) describes exemptions for informational materials and donations as part of the tariff proposals and says they are exempt; the operative note 52(a) (91 FR 47352) refers only to personal-use accompanied baggage. (7) The memorandum says TRQs 'will be feasible by September 1, 2026' (91 FR 47720, lines 221-223), while the operative section 2 says 'as soon as the Trade Representative determines that it is feasible' (91 FR 47320). The notice repeats the operative formula. The date is a projection in the recitals, not a deadline.
Q11.uncertainty: Several items turn on whether the Annex images contain exemptions that would reconcile them. I did not find an explicit statement that the 11064/11065 232 language is intended to supersede clause (2). I checked the forced-labor descriptions against the operative text and found no discrepancy in the rate descriptions for the economies in Q6.

Q13.answer: Machine on Annex I-C of 11032 (steel article), entered Oct 20, 2026 (within June 8, 2026 to Dec 31, 2027). Section 232 only. (a) Canada, USMCA claim, U.S. parts $60,000: non-U.S. content = $200,000 - $60,000 = $140,000; 25% x $140,000 = $35,000. The 15% floor is $30,000, which is lower, so $35,000. (b) No U.S. content: 25% x $200,000 = $50,000. (c) Canada, no USMCA: clause (2)(a) 25% x $200,000 = $50,000. (d) Japan, MFN 2.5%: Column 1 is below 15%, so the additional rate is 15% - 2.5% = 12.5% x $200,000 = $25,000 (total with MFN 15%). (e) Canada, USMCA claim, U.S. parts $20,000 plus $30,000 of U.S.-smelted aluminum inside a Canadian part: non-U.S. content = $200,000 - $20,000 = $180,000; 25% x $180,000 = $45,000 (floor $30,000 not binding). The U.S.-smelted aluminum is not a part produced in the U.S., so it does not reduce non-U.S. content; clause (2)(c) (10%) is not met because the machine's steel is not entirely U.S.-melted and the 85% rule of clause (4) is not met. (f) As (e), entered Oct 6, 2026: same answer, $45,000. (g) Canada, USMCA, U.S. parts $140,000: non-U.S. content $60,000; 25% x $60,000 = $15,000; the 15% floor of $30,000 applies, so $30,000. (h) The clause (2)(d) treatment applies from 12:01 a.m. June 8, 2026 through 11:59 p.m. EST Dec 31, 2027 (clause (2) of 11032). From 12:01 a.m. Jan 1, 2028, clause (3)(a) applies the rates in clause (3) of Proclamation 11021 (25% generally; 15% for UK products with UK-melted or UK-smelted metal; 10% where the metal is entirely U.S.-smelted or -melted), with no USMCA content formula in that clause.

Q14.answer: 1. Partly correct: the memorandum does not set a deadline of September 1. It says the USTR informed the President that establishing the TRQs 'is not feasible at this time, but ... will be feasible by September 1, 2026' (a projection). Its operative section 2 says the USTR shall establish the TRQs 'as soon as ... feasible'. 2. Incorrect: USTR received over 1,600 written comments and over 100 witnesses testified. 3. Incorrect: five economies moved from 12.5% to 10% flat (Honduras, India, Sri Lanka and Trinidad and Tobago because each adopted a ban after June 5; Jordan on its ART commitment). Seven is wrong. The EU and Taiwan changed to net-of-MFN 10%; Japan, Korea and Switzerland changed to net-of-MFN 12.5%. 4. Incorrect as stated: the notice records only that commenters opposed exempting beef and avocados (91 FR 47331). It does not say they were removed from the exempt list. 5. Incorrect: Japan's determination refers only to Annex I and Annex II Part A, the general list for any economy (47326, 47395), so Japan has no economy-specific list; the EU, Switzerland and Taiwan do have their own parts. 6. Partly correct: USTR added 471 products 'in each investigation' (47331, lines 1648-1649), and the list includes 'certain sugar and sugar containing products' (line 1667). 'All sugar' is not stated. 7. Incorrect: the notice contains no 'no product more than 12.5 percent' statement. For flat-rate economies the 301 duty is added to MFN; for net-of-MFN economies the total is capped only where the MFN rate is below the cap (and products with MFN above the cap are not reduced). 8. Correct: 91 FR 47321, lines 489-495: products admitted to an FTZ must be admitted as privileged foreign status unless eligible for domestic status, effective as of the date the duty is imposed. 9. Not stated: the severability section (91 FR 47335, lines 2122-2132) says that if a court holds a tariff action invalid, only that aspect is treated as invalid and the remainder continues. It does not say that the goods covered by an invalid exemption become subject to the duty. 10. Correct on the notice's own statement: USTR exempted all proposed Annex A products 'except the non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products' (91 FR 47330, lines 1539-1541; chemicals limited to pharmaceutical uses at lines 1577-1578). The Annex A list itself is an image.
Q14.basis: FR Doc 2026-15274 (91 FR 47720, lines 221-223; 47320 section 2); FR Doc 2026-15181: 47319 lines 218-221; 47324 (Honduras, India); 47327 (Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago, Jordan at 47324); 47331 (beef, avocados, 471 products, sugar); 47326 (Japan); 47321 (FTZ); 47335 (severability); 47330 (Annex A exemptions and chemicals); FR Doc 2026-11296 (91 FR 34274-34276) for the June proposal.
Q14.uncertainty: Annex A and the other exemption lists are images, so I could not check item 10 against the list itself, nor the sugar and beef/avocado lists. Item 9 is an inference from the text.
